title: Ben Pollack's record misrepresented the band
summary: Handy says the Pollack release gave listeners something else than the band's real music, and Boyd let it happen.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: I think so, because there was a lot of talk going around the whole

country about the band, about how interesting it was and about the new music that it was playing; then the country never got to hear the music. They were given something else, which they must have thought this is what they're talking about and that wasn't what people were talking about, at all. the ones that had heard the band, So it was total misrepresentation by not giving them what they were supposed to hear. They were given another item entirely.

To me it was dishonest and misleading and that's what happens when a commercial publisher who is looking to make money on pop tunes records the damn thing, just hoping that it's going to sell a lot of records and make him money on his royalties, not thinking of the future of the band, or what it's going to do for the band.
Did Pollack have any money in the band?
He was the guy that was recording it, he was the guy that had the publishing rights.
Did Boyd argue the point, or do you knww?

I can't believe that he did. I can only believe that he accepted whatever Pollack wanted and went along with him. Boyd was not a leader; not only not a musical leader, he was not a leader of men. He really was a wishy-washy type of guy who people lead around by the nose, and this is, I believe, what Ben Pollack did for the Boyd Raeburn band. He stopped it right at its moment of greatest push forward, stopped it cold. And could they believe that Johnny Richards was going to replace the music I had written?
